newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Western ad agencies get it wrong in Asia - IAA.
newsitem.headline: Western ad agencies get it wrong in Asia - IAA.

text.p: Many Western advertising agencies that have rushed to Asia to cash in on the world's fastest-growing consumer markets are making mistakes and hurting their prospects in the region, a top industry expert said.

Sonyon Kim, worldwide president of the International Advertising Association (IAA), the biggest global advertising body, told Reuters several agencies were getting it wrong by changing their staff too often.
"Patience is the key to success" in Asia, he said in an interview in Amsterdam late on Thursday.

"Often there is no continuity" at the Asian headquarters of big Western-based ad agency networks, he said, adding this sends the wrong message to local clients and consumers about the networks' long-term commitment to Asian markets .
"Suddenly the general manager is gone and the whole team is fired," he said after the opening of the IAA's annual European conference.

Kim, who is chairman and CEO of Sonyon Communications Inc, a South Korean agency, and chairman of Leo Burnett Sonyon Inc, the joint venture between his agency and Chicago-based Leo Burnett, became the first Asian last year to be appointed world president of the New York-based IAA.

"What I say to the global advertising agencies is: 'You're great. You have expertise -- but it's with the European markets and the American market. In Asia you have to establish local expertise'," he said.

"The most serious companies know they have to have a deep understanding of the (Asian) market, of consumers there. They are not American consumers. They are not European consumers. They are Asian consumers.
"They (Western-based ad agencies) must understand the culture. A deep understanding of the culture will smooth the way for cooperative communications," Kim said.

He said U.S.- and European-based agencies had to send expatriates to run their Asian offices in the past because there was a lack of local expertise. But that was no longer necessary, since a growing number of Asians with training in marketing- related services in the West were returning to Asia.

David Koedijk, the managing director of Henkel Benelux, part of the German-based chemicals and consumer products group, said many multinational companies were finding it increasingly difficult to persuade executives to work for a few years in Asia and other emerging markets.

"(It is) difficult to find Europeans for jobs in joint ventures in Asia. Many companies have problems in finding the right people for expatriate assignments in underdeveloped countries," he said in a speech at the IAA conference on Thursday.
Kim told Reuters that Asia would continue to have the world's fastest-growing advertising industry through the next century, with China and India the most important new markets.
"You should realise how quickly China is liberalising in every (business sector). The advertising industry is a good barometer of that," he said.

Japan has Asia's largest advertising industry and the second biggest in the world after the United States. South Korea is the second largest in Asia and the seventh worldwide, but it will be surpassed by the year 2000 by China, where the advertising sector is growing by 60 to 70 percent a year, Kim said.
He said huge industrial conglomerates in Asia like South Korea's "chaebol" were beginning to adopt Western-style marketing strategies by promoting their brands in Europe and the United States.

"I really welcome this trend. The American companies have taken a long time to try to understand Asian markets. In the same way, Asian multinationals have taken a long time to learn international marketing (techniques)," Kim said.
"It's taken a long time to convince them they have to understand the Western way, the American way of marketing."
Companies like Hyundai Corp, Daewoo Group and LG Lucky Goldstar are spending increasing amounts of money on advertising in the West.
"At first they just manufactured goods," Kim said. "Lately they've started marketing their goods. And now they're starting to say: 'Hey, we haven't promoted our brand name. Let's do that.' ".
